# Abstract \[needed for conferences\]

Rationality has been one of the most central and extensively debated
concepts in economics since the early twentieth century. Its centrality
partly stems from its multiple meanings and the diverse ways in which
economists have employed the term. Given the long and complex history of
such a widely used concept, bibliometric analysis and text mining offer
valuable tools for gaining a clearer understanding of the evolution of
its meanings and uses. Drawing on a large database of full-text
economics articles (approximately 300,000), we propose the use of large
language models (LLMs), such as BERT, to examine semantic shifts over
more than a century of economic publications. LLMs also facilitate the
identification of a corpus of texts centered on rationality, which can
then be analyzed through bibliometrics and network analysis. Our
objectives are threefold: (1) to map the different uses and meanings of
the terms “rationality” and “rational” over time; (2) to trace the
emergence of new uses and meanings; and (3) to identify the major
intellectual influences shaping these new uses and meanings.

# Long abstract \[needed for conferences\]

Rationality has been one of the most central and extensively debated
concepts in economics since the early twentieth century. From decision
theory, expected utility theory, to rational expectations, many
subfields of economics have their specific history of a complex
relationship with the concept of rationality. Beyond the inner
contributions of the discipline, interdisciplinary exchanges and
controversies between economics and other social sciences have often
taken rationality as a central point of departure to discuss the
epistemological boundaries of economics.

While we find a few existing attempts at writing the history of
rationality in economics, it is a daunting task to tackle such a large
object. Typically, existing histories are often fragmented and focus on
one particular subfield in relation to rationality, such as the rise of
rational expectations in macroeconomics or the emergence of behavioral
economics with Kahneman and Tversky’s contributions. In addition,
although such histories often identify clear milestones such as the
publication of canonical articles, the exact timing and scale of these
transformations often remain uncertain.

We provide a pedagogical methodological blueprint for using quantitative
tools to tackle such historical themes. Our goal is to show historians
of economics how these tools can help address their own research
questions, but also how they may help open new lines of inquiry. For
this purpose, we focus on the history of rationality in economics
because its centrality captures the interest of many historians of
different subfields of economics, but also because existing attempts at
writing a general history of rationality in economics often proved
underdeveloped in some aspects.

In the present article, we apply scientometric and natural language
processing techniques to a large corpus of twentieth and
twenty-first-century economic literature, mixing JSTOR full-text data
with Web of Science bibliometric data to study the history of
rationality in economics. From simple techniques that historians can
integrate into their everyday research to more advanced tools reserved
for specialized investigations, we will tackle what quantitative
approaches can and can’t do for historians. Our analysis showcases how
these methods can pinpoint the timing and scale of conceptual shifts,
measure the influence of key texts, and map the relationships of
different sub-fields of economics concerning rationality.

# Introduction

Several essays have examined the emergence of quantitative methods in
the history of economics (Cherrier and Andrej; Edwards et al., etc.). A
common limitation of these programmatic contributions lies in the
generality of their discussions. Given the virtually unlimited number of
quantitative methods potentially relevant to historians of economics—as
well as the wide array of research questions these methods can
address—these reflections often remain abstract and offer little in the
way of concrete or practical guidance. As a result, they tend to provide
broad overviews without clearly articulating what quantification entails
in practice, and how it can be both meaningful and challenging to
integrate into historical research.

# **A literature review on the history of rationality**

Rationality is perhaps one of the most central and encompassing concepts
in economics, alongside “market” and “competition”. Several
contributions have offered broad narratives tracing its evolution over
several decades or within specific subfields of economics. Moreover, a
substantial body of work by historians of economics has focused on
specific concepts—such as the emergence of expected utility theory, the
development of rational expectations, and the evolution of bounded
rationality. Our aim in this section is not to provide an exhaustive
summary of all historical contributions on the concept of rationality,
but rather to highlight key developments and debates in this long and
complex history.

The idea that economic agents behave in a rational way was already
implicit in many classical arguments, such as the Ricardian theory of
rent, where farmers rationally select land according to its marginal
fertility and profitability. While it is probably vain to look for a
single precise origin of the concept in economics, it certainly gained
prominence with the rise of scientific and abstract reasoning in the
late nineteenth century. The question of rational behavior was closely
intertwined with the broader issue of the proper scope of economic
analysis (Giocoli 2003). A well-known example is John Stuart Mill, who
in *Essays on Some Unsettled Questions of Political Economy* wrote:

> “What is now commonly understood by the term ‘Political Economy’ is
> not the science of speculative politics, but a branch of that science.
> It does not treat the whole of man’s nature as modified by the social
> state, nor of the whole conduct of man in society. It is concerned
> with him solely as a being who desires to possess wealth, and who is
> capable of judging the comparative efficacy of means for obtaining
> that end.” (Mill, 1848)

With the marginalist the economic agent was increasingly conceived in
terms of calculative ability—for instance, Jevons portrayed him as a
calculating machine balancing pleasures and pains that would eventually
be formalized by the hypothesis of utility maximization (Maas, 1999).
From marginalist theory, therefore, a first meaning of rationality
crystallized around the idea of utility maximization. Based on the
fundamental psychological premise that agents are self-interested,
rational behavior was understood as the consistent selection of those
means that maximize utility given available constraints.

The Second World War and the Cold War was a critical turning point in
the development of the concept of “rationality” (Erickson et al.,
Mirowski). The key institutions in the Cold War context and the
emergence of the concept of “rationality” were the RAND corporation
(Erickson et al) and the Cowles Commission (Herfeld). Both were central
to the development of operations research and linear programming in the
late 1940s, involving figures such as Jacob Marschak, Tjalling Koopmans
or George Dantzig (Duppe and Weintraub 2014). These developments, in
turn, played a central role in helping Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu
to establish the proof of the existence of a general equilibrium in an
economy composed of rational agents (Duppe and Weintraub book; Kirtchik
and Boldyrev). Through these contributions, the concept of rationality
came to be distinguished from concepts such as “reason” (Erickson et
al.) or “intelligence” (Klaes and Sent). Rationality emerged as a formal
concept, independent of personality or context, materializing through a
set of “rigid rules that determine unique solutions” (Erickson et al.
2013, 3). From this axiomatic tradition emerged a second meaning of
rationality, centered on the idea of consistent choice: agents were
considered rational insofar as their preferences—whatever their
psychological origins—satisfied a set of formal conditions that
guaranteed internal coherence (Giocoli 2003).

At the individual level, the 1940s also marked a turning point in the
formalization and axiomatization of economic behavior, most notably
through the development of expected utility theory by Oskar Morgenstern
and John Von Neumann in *Theory of Games and Economic Behavior*
(Morgenstern and Von Neumaan, Leonard …). Morgenstern and Von Neumann
formulated a set of axioms governing individual preferences
(transitivity, completeness, independence, etc…) which allowed for the
derivation of a value function capable of ordering agents’ choices
(Moscati 2023). Leonard Savage (1954) extended this framework by
developing subjective expected utility theory, which addressed
decision-making under uncertainty—that is when objective probabilities
are not known.

Such modeling quickly developed along two dimensions: a positive one,
seeking to represent how agents behave in the “real world,” and a
normative one, concerned with identifying optimal procedures for
decision-making (Herfeld, Hands). As rationality came to be redefined in
terms of *consistent choice* rather than as an empirical description of
the *Homo Oeconomicus*, the normative dimension expanded the discussion
beyond individual behavior to encompass broader issues of social choice
and the design of “rationalizing” policies.

Another key institution in the history of the concept of rationality in
economics was the Graduate School in Industrial Administration at the
Carnegie Institute of Technology (Klein 2015). With funding from the
Office of Naval Research obtained in the 1950s, a team of GSIA
economists—including Charles Holt, Franco Modigliani, John Muth and
Herbert Simon—was tasked with focusing on the theory of the firm and
improving methods for production and inventory planning. This project
was pivotal in the emergence of both Simon’s concept of “bounded
rationality” and Muth’s “rational expectations” (Sent, 2002). While
Muth’s concept was initially intended for use in microeconomic analysis
of firm behavior, it was soon adopted and further developed by Robert
Lucas and Edward Prescott (1971), both at GSIA at the time, and by
Thomas Sargent (Darity et al., Duarte, 2025). Rational expectations
quickly became a highly debated concept in a variety of theoretical
frameworks requiring forward-looking behavior—for instance, in
macroeconomics where it became the foundation component of dynamic
stochastic general equilibrium (Goutsmedt et al.; Sergi 2020) or in
finance (Delcey & Sergi 2020). While the rational expectations
hypothesis was gaining popularity after the 1970s, expected utility
theories were, during the same period, increasingly
challenged—particularly through critiques rooted in paradoxes of
rationality raised by Maurice Allais (1953) or Daniel Ellsberg (1961;
see e.g. Zappia 2018). These critiques notably contributed to the
development of Prospect Theory by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky
(1979), and the subsequent rise of behavioral economics (Truc, …). In
this context, “bounded rationality” experienced renewed interest after
the 1980s (Sent 2018).

This history of the different meanings and uses of the concept of
rationality is also a history of changing methods. It reflects shifts in
both mathematical techniques and conceptions of rationality itself: a
passage from a “system-of-forces”—analyzying “economic processes
generated by market and non-market forces” (Gioccoli, 4)— to a
“system-of-relations,” in which the “main subject is the investigation
of the existence and properties of economic equilibria in terms of the
validation and mutual consistency of given formal conditions (5). In
this transformation, mathematical methods and tools, such as
axiomatization and fixed-point theorems became central to the discipline
of economics (Weintraub 2002, Herfeld 2017). Game theory also
progressively found its place in economics, even though it remained
marginal in the years immediately following Morgenstern and Von
Neumann's *Theory of Games and Economic Behavior* (Gioccoli 2003,
Erickson 2015). The history of rationality is also the history of new
alliances between economics and engineering. The work of Holt,
Modigliani, Simon and Muth facilitated the importation of control theory
into economics (Klein 2015), while the new classical economics—Lucas,
Prescott, and Sargent—introduced elements of “information engineering,”
inspired by information theory (Boumans 2020). Finally, this history of
the concept of rationality also intersects with the so-called “applied
turn” in economics (Backhouse and Cherrier): challenges to expected
utility theories coincided with an increasing reliance on experimental
methods—an approach that became central to the development of behavioral
economics (Truc…).

What can the use of quantitative methods contribute to this already rich
historiography? Many contributions have focused on the pioneering works
of scientists like Von Neumann, Koopmans or Arrow. However, as Gioccoli
(2003, PP) has emphasized, the fact that these foundational
contributions were developed in the 1940s and 1950s does not imply that
new conceptions of rationality were immediately adopted. The timing and
diffusion of such “innovations” remain complex issues in the history of
science that we seek to investigate. Moreover, the exponential growth in
publications after the 1970s has likely multiplied the meanings and
applications of “rationality,” making it increasingly difficult to
construct a comprehensive picture. We offer a broader perspective on the
diverse uses and interpretations of the concept, beyond the foundational
texts that explicitly engage with rationality. This challenge is all the
more significant given the concept’s proliferation across
subfields—including general equilibrium theory, game theory,
macroeconomics, and behavioral economics—as well as areas where
rationality plays a less direct but still influential role, such as
finance, firm behavior, public economics, social choice and welfare
economics, as well as political economy and institutional economics. In
addition, the concept is tied to distinct methods, formalizations, and
mathematical tools, further complicating efforts to map its evolution.

This article does not aim to provide a definitive history of
rationality—far from it—but rather to offer a series of snapshots
illustrating how quantitative methods can confirm established historical
findings, challenge or refine others, and expand the scope of historical
inquiry.

# **Which methods and which challenges ?**

Historians of economics today have at their disposal an expanding set of
quantitative tools—from, for instance, traditional statistical
inference, machine learning, textual analysis, network analysis and
bibliometrics. Recent discussions of the “quantitative turn” in the
history and philosophy of economics have focused on weighing the pros
and cons of these methods, stressing their complementarity with
qualitative approaches, and speculating about the future of this
relationship. Yet most of these reflections remain at a general level,
offering broad overviews of techniques that risk being too abstract to
give readers a concrete sense of what quantitative analysis actually
entails in practice. We take a different path. In our view, what matters
most is to examine what kinds of questions and challenges quantitative
analysis raises at each stage of the research process. To do so, we
ground the discussion in our own inquiry into the history of rationality
in economics. This concrete focus allows us to emphasize (a) the crucial
issue of sources and data; (b) how even simple quantitative assessments
can be highly informative; (c) the various challenges and subjective
choice involved in building and adapting tools; and (d) why the
interpretation of results requires a careful study of various indicators
and a fine-grained knowledge of both the corpus and its historical
context. By following step by step the process of assembling and
analyzing our corpus, we aim to provide both a practical example and a
reflection on the broader methodological issues faced by quantitative
historians.

## From raw source to data 

Discussions on quantitative methods often focus on the varieties of
methods existing and their relationship to qualitative analysis. Yet,
despite often relying on sophisticated techniques, analysis and
interpretation are usually the last—and not always the most
difficult—step. It is not unusual for most of the time to be devoted to
data collection and wrangling, even if much of this work remains
invisible in the final paper. Our corpus of interest is rarely available
in a ready-to-use database but rather as raw sources that need to be
structured. In a nutshell, a quantitative historian must be as much a
skilled data wrangler as a data analyst.

The first step is to find the data. In our case, we want a comprehensive
collection of economic documents that may discuss the concept of
rationality and we want to know how the concept is actually used in
these discussions. A well-structured category of sources at our disposal
are bibliometric databases that index research documents. One of their
main advantages is that they provide relatively well-structured data,
systematically categorizing key features of scientific output—such as
authors, journals and affiliations, etc.. In addition, some of these
databases record citation data, which enables the study of intellectual
influence, diffusion patterns, and the structure of scholarly
communication. One crucial missing element, however, is the text itself.
If some textual features are available, such as the title and for the
most recent periods the abstracts, the full text in which the discussion
is actually taking place is generally missing or very costly. One
exception is JSTOR that provides us X full texts of documents covering
the period between 1900 and 2020.

Before proceeding, we step back to a methodological point: how the
available data shape what we can ask—and answer—about rationality. The
scarcity and structure of available data already affects our multiple
stages of the research process, from the selection of research questions
to the answers we provide. In practice, our research may be shaped as
much by the availability of our data as by our own research preferences.
In our case, Figures X show that our full-text database, like most
available databases, disproportionately represents Anglo-Saxon economic
journals, which are also those most systematically digitized and
preserved. Not only do we tend to overlook other traditions of economic
research, but this also raises a serious issue of presentism: the fact
that these journals are visible in recent periods does not imply that
they were equally central in earlier ones, nor that articles were the
dominant vehicle for the diffusion of ideas. Rather, it reflects the
fact that they had the resources and opportunities to digitize and
maintain comprehensive digital archives of their publications. Moreover,
several key economics journals are absent from JSTOR (e.g. *Ecological
Economics, Energy Policy*, *Applied Economics*), while other
bibliometric databases such as Web of Science or Scopus present their
own limitations in coverage and accessibility[^1]

Figure X: Distribution of languages in the JSTOR fulltext database

Once access to JSTOR full text is secured, another crucial step is to
transform them into a usable database. In most cases, data are not
readily available in a structured format; rather, they result from a
process that involves cleaning, categorizing, and selectively removing
or reformatting information from raw sources in order to produce a
dataset suitable for computational analysis. This challenge is
particularly true in the history of economics, where the primary sources
are the texts themselves—often unstructured and interspersed with
various layers of metadata, such as section headings, footnotes,
bibliographic references, or editorial annotations.

\[Figure X: image of raw text ?\]

We do not mean, however, to imply that data wrangling is a necessary but
laborious step before “real” historical analysis begins. On the
contrary, manipulating, cleaning, and structuring raw sources is both a
fundamental and stimulating stage of the research process. As recalled
by Lemercier and Zalc (2018, 62), the collection and categorisation of
sources is also “a moment to reflect on the sources and the purpose of
the research.” It is a potentially creative moment in which the direct
confrontation with raw data permits the reevaluation of initial
hypotheses and the emergence of new questions. In our case, the cleaning
and structuring of full-text documents raises many questions about what
should be offered as input of our analysis, and consequently, what
counts as a relevant economic text. Should we include book reviews,
editorials, or working papers or conference proceedings ? And how do we
define what qualifies as an economic journal—should it be restricted to
the traditional “core” journals, or extended to interdisciplinary ones
where economics frequently appears? Even within a single article, the
boundary of what may be the textual content to analyze is not always
clear: should headings, abstracts, footnotes, appendix or
acknowledgements be treated as part of the text or definitely excluded?
Each of these decisions have important historiographical implications.
It shapes the boundaries of our corpus and, ultimately, the history of
rationality that our methods can reveal. There is rarely a single,
definitive choice, but rather a series of trade-offs that must be made
explicit

The first important choice we made was to restrict our analysis to
English articles, because cross-language comparisons remain difficult.
Cross-language textual analysis is challenging since most quantitative
methods are designed to identify commonalities within texts that share a
specific linguistic structure. Hence, the same topic discussed by two
documents in two different languages will likely not be identified as
related, since the language differences obscure their underlying
semantic similarity**.** We also restrain our analysis to research
articles and filter out book reviews, comments, editorial reports or
obituaries. While some of these secondary documents may contain
important information on the way rationality was debated, they are not
sites of enunciation of new ideas within the discipline. Moreover,
textual data are by nature heavy, and filtering documents make the
overall corpus more tractable for large-scale computational methods. At
the level of documents, we focused on the body text, removing peripheral
elements such as acknowledgements, references, or appendices.

## Studying Rationality through Texts

Once the corpus has been assembled, the next challenge is to identify
how the concept of rationality is actually used in the texts. A
straightforward first step is simply to measure the frequency of
occurrence of the terms themselves. Figure X, for instance, shows the
relative frequency (with respect to the total number of words published
each year) of “rational” and “rationality.” The figure reveals a clear
surge in the 1980s and 1990s, suggesting that discussions explicitly
framed in terms of rationality became particularly prominent during this
period.

<img src="figs/media/image3.png"
style="width:6.26772in;height:3.76389in" />

Figure X: The relative frequency of terms of “rational” and
“rationality”.

But the key question is not only whether a document contains the word
“rationality,” but rather what meaning the term takes in its specific
context. In other words, we are less interested in mere keyword
retrieval than in uncovering the different meanings and intellectual
settings in which rationality is invoked. A simple way to begin
addressing this question is through co-occurrence analysis, that is, by
looking at the neighboring words that most often appear alongside
“rational” or “rationality.” Co-occurences provide clues about the
conceptual frames and debates in which the term was embedded. Figure X,
for example, displays the five words that most frequently appear
immediately before or after 'rational' and 'rationality' in each decade,
highlighting how the associations of rationality shifted over time.
Before the 1940s, the picture is rather heterogeneous: rationality is
connected to a variety of terms, often closer to philosophy, psychology,
or general notions of reasoning. From the 1940s onward, however, the
emergence of choice theory brought rationality to the center of economic
modeling, particularly as a way to describe and formalize human
behavior. By the 1970s and especially the 1980s, the framework itself
was being refined and challenged, with the appearance of notions such as
rational expectations on the one hand, and bounded rationality on the
other.

<img src="figs/media/image2.png"
style="width:6.26772in;height:4.18056in" />

Figures X: DRAFT TO CLEAN (the top neighbor words of terms of “rational”
and “rationality”)

While co-occurrence analysis already provides insights into the
evolution of rationality, it remains limited to a broad picture of the
immediate lexical environment of a word. Such methods capture proximity
in vocabulary, not necessarily proximity in meaning. For example, one
sentence may speak of “rational behavior” while another refers to
“profit maximization”: they share no terms, yet they clearly point to
closely related conceptions of agency and choice.

To move from this broad picture to how each document actually mobilizes
the concept—and to map semantic relationships that are not visible
through shared keywords—we turn to recent advances in natural language
processing, in particular to large language models (LLMs). These models
represent text in ways that encode context and meaning, enabling us to
compare sentences that are semantically similar even when their
vocabularies diverge. Similarly, it allows us to see how the same word
may have different meanings when its context of use changes. Although
quantitative text analysis is not new, its scope has expanded with these
methods. Before introducing our LLM‑based approach, we take a step back
to present the basic principles of text representation because these
principles remain relatively unfamiliar in the history of economics.

One of the most crucial concepts in textual analysis is the text
*representation*, that is how text units (words, paragraphs, sentences,
etc.) are encoded into numbers that can be processed by a computer. The
most basic and historically the most dominant representation was the
bag-of-word representation. Imagine a corpus in which your unit of
interest is the document. You may want, for instance, to gather similar
documents together to make sense of your corpus. But how can you compare
documents computationally, if texts are made of words and computers only
process numbers ? The *bag-of-words* representation provides a simple
solution: it transforms each document into a vector of word counts. Each
dimension of this vector corresponds to a specific word from the
vocabulary, and its value reflects how many times that word appears in
the document. Two documents that use many of the same words will have
similar vectors that can be computed. This representation is, for
instance, the representation used in the probabilistic topic models that
became increasingly used in the history of economics (Ambrosino et al.;
Truc and Goutsmedt, etc.).

Any representation transforms a rich source of natural language into a
simplified numerical format and, inevitably, loses some of the
complexity and nuance of meaning along the way. A crucial question,
then, is: what kind of information is preserved, and what is lost ?
Because it focuses only on the frequency of words, the *bag-of-words*
representation discards two essential dimensions of language: context
(i.e., the surrounding words) and word order. A document is represented
as a bag in which words are blindly tossed. For instance, the two
sentences “Hayek is right and Keynes is wrong” and “Hayek is wrong and
Keynes is right” have exactly the same bag-of-words representation for a
computer whilst having opposite meaning for humans.

A major breakthrough that overcomes these limitations has been the
development of world embeddings (Mikolov et al. 2013). While the
bag-of-words model represents texts as unordered vectors of word counts,
word embeddings focus on representing *individual* words in a way that
captures their semantic relationships. Embeddings represent each word as
a point in a vector space, learned from patterns of word co-occurrence
in a large corpora of texts.[^2] Figure X illustrates this principle. We
simulate word vectors in a two-dimensional space. In reality, embeddings
exist in high-dimensional spaces, but the principle is the same:
absolute positions are arbitrary, while relative distances encode
semantic relationships. Words that are plotted closer are more similar
in meaning, even if they rarely co-occur.

<img src="figs/media/image5.png"
style="width:6.26772in;height:4.63889in" />

Figures Y: Illustration of a two dimension projection of word
embeddings.

The first generation of embedding models, such as Word2Vec or GloVe,
learned static word vectors: each word had a single position in the
vector space, regardless of the sentences or documents in which it
appears. This makes it more difficult to grasp differences in meanings
of a same word. The more recent generation of embedding models, known as
LLMs, builds on a different principle: rather than assigning a fixed
vector to each word, they produce contextualized embeddings—that is,
vectors that depend on the surrounding words (the context). In LLMs, the
meaning of the word “rationality,” captured by a word embedding vector,
may vary significantly depending on the contexts in which it is used in
the studied corpus. Each vector captures an usage of rationality based
on the contexts in which different authors wrote. In this way, ideas and
conceptual transformations become measurable and quantifiable objects,
opening new possibilities for the study of economic ideas.

We use Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019), a variant of the LLM
BERT, designed to produce sentence embeddings rather than word
embeddings. This model yields a single vector representation per
sentence, which allows straightforward semantic comparison by measuring
the similarity between sentence vectors. To illustrate how embedding
vectors capture semantic information, we compare the real sentences from
the database with a synthetic sentence: *“Economic agents are supposed
to be rational.”* Table X reports the most similar sentences retrieved
for various years.[^3]

| **year** | **sentences in our corpus** | **similarity** |
|----|----|----|
| 1950 | Basically, for Professor Hicks, as for Jevons and Marshall, economic decisions are made by an abstract calculating machine. | 0.7056321 |
| 1950 | Modern civilization is lopsided in its emphasis on rationality, especially on economic rationality. | 0.7001227 |
| 1950 | Rational behavior means conduct motivated by the goal of maximization of money income, wealth and economic advantages. | 0.7000580 |
| 1975 | Rationality and Irrationality in Economics. | 0.7499573 |
| 1975 | Such agents are assumed to act rationally and exclusively on the basis of market given information. | 0.7211479 |
| 1975 | In Marshallian analysis, economic agents are conceived to be not so much rational as reasonable. | 0.7097100 |
| 2000 | Agents have rational expectations. | 0.7705028 |
| 2000 | Rational in the narrow economic sense of profit maximizing. | 0.7678480 |
| 2000 | Actors who operate in an economy are generally rational in the sense that they are interested in improving their individual position. | 0.7676246 |

Table 1: Closest to ‘Economic agents are supposed to be rational.’

We vectorized more than 31 millions of sentences from the JSTOR database
using Sentence-BERT. Our objective is to identify sentences that discuss
rationality and related concepts. Rather than relying solely on the
presence of the keyword *rationality*, we use cosine similarit**y**
between sentence vectors to detect semantic proximity. For instance, if
sentence A explicitly mentions *rationality* and its vector is close to
the vector of sentence B—which does not use the term—it is likely that B
addresses a related idea.

A straightforward first approach would be to compute a single average
embedding vector for all sentences containing the word *rationality* or
*rational*, and to use this as a representative embedding for the
concept. However, such an average would be present-biased: since the
number of documents in the corpus grows sharply over time, the average
would be disproportionately influenced by recent decades, thereby
over-emphasizing contemporary meanings of *rationality* at the expense
of older ones. To account for potential semantic shifts over time, we
compute a moving average vector for each year, using a sliding window of
five years (i.e., the year in question plus five years before and
after). From 1900 to 2020, this method yields 120 yearly representative
vectors, each reflecting the evolving contextual meaning of
*rationality* in the economic literature. For each year, we then
computed the similarity between sentences from the corpus and the
respective representative vector and we kept the 1% closest sentences (X
sentences).

<img src="figs/media/image1.png"
style="width:3.69427in;height:2.21656in" />

\[Figure C: Distribution of the 1% closest sentences to representative
vector by year\]

We interpret these sentences as reflecting how economists mobilize the
concept of rationality, in different historical contexts. Because of the
huge number of sentences we have identified, we would like a method to
group sentences using a similar meaning of rationality together. We then
cluster the sentences using the K-means algorithm—one of the most widely
used and straightforward methods for grouping LLM embeddings. Because
the distribution of our identified sentences is present-biased (Figure
C), we cannot run a clustering algorithm on the entire distribution
without risking clusters being over-determined by recent periods. We
therefore run a clustering algorithm separately for each decade since
1900 (merging the first two decades because of the small number of
observations). Table 2 provides a concrete example of what we mean by a
cluster. We selected two clusters—respectively from the 1980s and
1990s—and report the three sentences nearest to the representative
vector for each cluster, along with metadata from the associated
documents. Note that these textual clusters group sentences rather than
documents; hence, a single document can, in principle, contribute to
several meanings of rationality. Despite being arbitrarily separated by
decade, it is clear that sentences in both clusters convey a very
similar meaning of rationality centered on the concept of rational
expectations. To capture this stability of meanings across time, we
merge clusters between decades when their sentences are sufficiently
close. Following this procedure, the two clusters presented in Table 2
are ultimately merged into a single, temporally continuous cluster.
Figure X displays the complete set of results in the form of an alluvial
plot.

\[INSERT ALLUVIAL TEXT ANALYSIS\]

To ensure the stability of our results, we compare them with a
bibliometric analysis of the corpus. Such a comparison is not costless,
but it is highly recommended for at least two reasons. First, crossing
the results of advanced computational methods such as LLM embeddings
serves as a form of robustness check.[^4] Second, the systematic
comparison of sources and methods is a fundamental principle of
historical analysis. As we already discussed, each source has its
strengths and limitations, and confronting them against each other helps
to overcome individual biases. For instance, we saw that our JSTOR
full-text database, while comprehensive, does not index several crucial
recent journals in economics—a gap that can be partly compensated by
crossing it with citation databases. Moreover, while full texts provide
invaluable insights into the meanings and contexts of concepts, citation
data highlight patterns of direct intellectual influence and diffusion.
On the one hand, we focus on the semantic uses of rationality and
related discussions in the text themselves, independently of authors'
institutional proximity or their citation practice. On the other hand,
with the bibliometric analysis, we look rather at how these ideas
circulated and have been diffused across fields.

## Studying rationality through citations

Beyond textual analysis, another important source of information are the
features (or metadata) of the documents (e.g., authors, institutions,
citations). We focus here on citations to study how authors cite and are
cited. While textual data focus on the instantiation of an idea,
citations rather allow us to understand its lineages and diffusion. The
evolution of an idea often depends as much on how it is circulated and
appropriated by readers as on how it was first formulated by its
authors.

One major issue for quantitative analysts using this method is temporal:
since systematic citation practices are relatively recent, patterns of
bibliographic coupling are difficult to interpret before the 1960s and
practically impossible due to the poor quality of earlier data. In
contrast to textual analysis, thus, bibliometric approaches are largely
confined to the postwar period. A second limitation is again the
scarcity and quality of data: categorizing references from thousands of
documents is a complex, time-consuming, and often imperfect task—even if
recent efforts have been made to develop tools in this direction (see,
for instance, Goutsmedt anystyle \[X\]). This is why we rely on the Web
of Science database, one of the best available sources of structured
bibliometric data on publications and their references, although it is
proprietary, costly, and not openly accessible. In addition to accessing
citation data on most economic documents, we therefore augmented our
initial JSTOR full-text database with citation data from Web of Science,
as well as citation and abstract data from key journals missing in
JSTOR, as discussed in Section \#.

Citation data does not require sophisticated analysis to be relevant,
and can be easily incorporated into the everyday toolset of historians
of economics. Simply counting citations can be used to proxy engagement
and better understand the impact of a particular author or publication.
There are compelling reasons to incorporate citation studies in
historical research. Beyond serving as a proxy for the extent to which
ideas disseminate, highly cited papers are more visible and get more
engagement (Matthew Effect), and some recent studies suggest that
citations affect reading and citations patterns, as well as perception
of quality (Teplitskiy et al., 2022): highly cited papers have a higher
chance to be a “substantial intellectual influence”, and they are often
read more thoroughly because they are perceived as of better quality.

Historians commonly discuss the impact, influence, and scientific
recognition of the figures they study, often relying on proxies such as
major grants, prizes, or honors. For instance, Sent (2004) traces the
transition from the dominance of rational choice theory, to the failure
of “old” behavioral economics to bring psychology back in economics
(e.g., Simon, George Katona), to the rise of “new” behavioral economics
(e.g., Kahneman, Akerlof). Sent’s introduction and historical narrative
is structured around pivotal moments such as major grants, Nobel Prizes,
or the John Bates Clark medal. In this sense, citations can be seen as a
complementary proxy—alongside these more traditional markers—for
assessing impact and influence. In an extensive qualitative and
quantitative study of the Nobel Prize in economics, Offer and Söderberg
(2016) identify different groups among Nobel winners: some win the Nobel
at their peak in terms of citations, but rapidly decline after. Others
do not decline and are what they call “innovators with staying power”.
Some are “still rising” winners, who receive the prize early in their
career years before their peak, while a few are late winners who get the
Nobel way after their peak influence. Placing these institutional
rewards in relation to citation and publication patterns thus helps to
clarify how recognition interacts with the longer processes of
diffusion, reception, and appropriation of ideas.

To illustrate these points within our study of rationality, (Figure
\[BOUNDED\]) computes the citation patterns of four seminal references
in relation to bounded rationality in all economic journals and the top
five. While the four articles chosen are partly arbitrary, they are four
important publications discussed in the literature for different
reasons: Allais (1953) and Simon (1955) are some of the earliest
criticisms of neoclassical rational choice theory, which had both
empirical and normative implications. Akerlof (1970) and Kahneman and
Tversky (1979) are two of the earliest “new” behavioral economics
publications, partly capturing the field's emergence and subsequent
development.

Examining the citation patterns of these four articles raise interesting
elements in relation to several arguments prevalent in the literature.
First, the influence of "new" behavioral economics dramatically
overshadows that of "old" behavioral economics. This holds true both for
the top 5 economic journals and all economics journals indexed in Web of
Science. While Allais (1953) and Simon (1955) were never cited by more
than 0.20% of all economics articles within the studied period, Kahneman
and Tversky (1979) achieved at least 1% of all economics article
citations by the late 2010s and their influence continued to grow. The
difference in citation patterns informs us about both the scale of the
differentiated influence of “old” vs “new” behavioral economics, but
also the differentiated speed at which they gained acceptance. While the
rise of the two “new” behavioral economics articles was rapid and
relatively steady after their publication, Simon and Allais’ peak
citations were around the time they received the Nobel, or way later in
the 2010s. The peak citations around the Nobel are not surprising, as
argued by Offer and Söderberg (2016), most Nobel recipients received a
“Nobel premium”, that is a small bump in citations after receiving the
Nobel. However, while Allais and Simon display this small bump, we can
see that the case of Kahneman and Tversky (1979) is particularly extreme
as after the nobel, his citation trend switched from decreasing to
increasing with no stopping in sight over the period studied.

style="width:6.22396in;height:3.4997in" />

Figure \[BOUNDED\]: Citations of key references related to bounded
rationality

This late point brings another interesting fact rarely explored in the
literature. While it has often been argued that the rise of “new”
behavioral economics shadowed the pre-existing works of “old” behavioral
economics, Simon (1955) has never been more cited than after the rise of
“new” behavioral economics, and a similar observation can be made about
Allais (1953). This resurgence in citations allows for three
interpretations. The first, a more positive one, suggests that Sent's
aspiration for a "revival of abandoned research directions" or Peter
Earl’s (2022) wish for a reconciliation of old and new behavioral
economics was realized, with "new" behavioral economics indeed
stimulating a renewed interest for earlier ideas. A second, more
critical interpretation suggests a form of intellectual appropriation.
It posits that these "old" references were transformed and reinterpreted
to align with the "new" behavioral economics agenda. For example, while
Allais's critique of standard rationality encompassed both normative and
empirical dimensions, his work was arguably misconstrued by "new"
behavioral economists as primarily experimental. Thus, the rise of
behavioral economics may have renewed interest in older scholarship, but
potentially through a biased and presentist lens. Finally, a third and
the most critical interpretation posits that the citation increase is
evidence of a growing backlash against NBE from an OBE standpoint.
Scholars may be citing Simon and Allais to emphasize a core
philosophical divergence. Finally, a third and even more critical view
is that the rise in citations indicates a growing critique against “new”
behavioral economics, articulated from the perspective of “old”
behavioral economics.

While counting citations alone cannot settle which interpretation is
correct, it can orient qualitative reading and suggest further possible
quantitative work. Studying the citations patterns observed towards
Simon’s and other old behavioral economists with specialized and more
advanced quantitative tools could help differentiate the different way
theses references are used. This could be done by looking at the
journals, authors and communities citing these authors, and/or by
combining textual and citations data to identify if citations to Simon
are superficially used by “new” behavioral economics or used to leverage
a criticism of “new” behavioral economics by “old” behavioral economists
(see Cavalcanti et al., 2011 or Budi & Yaniasih, 2022 for example of
positive/negative citations classifications).

Beyond simple citation counts, citations can also be used in more
sophisticated and systematic ways to study relationships between authors
or publications. One prominent example is bibliographic coupling
analysis, an increasingly used method in the history of economics that
maps corpora of documents based on the proximity of their references.
The central hypothesis of bibliographic coupling is that similarity in
references reflects intellectual proximity between texts. Spatialized in
two dimensions, texts appear as nodes, and the more references they
share, the closer they are positioned. Mapping the relationship between
authors and publications is an important tool to delineate fields and
disciplines, but it can also reveal how they are structured—for example,
according to a core–periphery pattern.

To run a bibliographic coupling analysis, one major issue lies in the
delimitation of the corpus: which articles should be included in a
corpus about rationality? A straightforward solution is to rely on
keyword search queries; however, as we have already discussed,
keyword-based approaches present important limitations: for instance, it
is possible that an article on revealed preference or on the prospect
theory does not mention often or at all the words “rational” or
“rationality”. We use instead the features of our LLM model and JSTOR
sentences embedding. For each article in our coupled JSTOR–Web of
Science database, we compute the cosine similarity between its
embedding—obtained by averaging all the article’s sentence
embeddings—and the representative vector associated with its year of
publication. We then retain the 10% of documents that lie closest in
this semantic space, thereby selecting those most strongly engaged with
the uses of rationality at this specific year. Because embeddings
capture deeper patterns of meaning and association, we are able to
identify documents that engage with debates related to rationality even
when the word “rationality” itself does not explicitly appear in the
text. This approach allows us to construct a bibliometric corpus that
goes beyond keyword-based searches and traces the broader intellectual
conversations surrounding the concept of rationality.

We then applied the dynamic network analysis developed by Goutsmedt and
Truc (2022), which we present in detail in the appendix, that followed
the same spirit as the method we developed for sentence clusters.
Intuitively, this method does not produce a single network covering the
entire period, but rather a series of overlapping networks built on
smaller time windows to preserve historical accuracy. A clustering
algorithm is applied to each of these networks, and clusters are
subsequently merged across windows when they share a sufficient number
of nodes (documents). In a bibliographic coupling analysis, a cluster is
defined as a group of documents that share a significant proportion of
references, thereby indicating intellectual proximity. Hence, our
bibliometric cluster here reflects a group of documents that all discuss
rationality and that tends to discuss it with similar references. While
our LLM clusters capture semantic similarities at the level of
sentences, our bibliometric clusters instead reveal intellectual
lineages and shared citation practices at the level of documents.

After all these sophisticated analyses, however, an essential question
arises: what is the place of qualitative readings and the close
appreciation of our primary materials—texts and their ideas?

## Do you still need to read ?

A recurring criticism of quantitative analysis is that it distances
researchers from the economic ideas themselves. This view is misleading
for several reasons. First, as we already discussed, data wrangling
often requires a detailed engagement with texts. The very act of
transforming a raw source into structured data is not given but entails
many crucial decisions about cleaning, categorizing, or excluding
materials. This requires a fine understanding of the corpus and a good
knowledge of the context in which the texts were produced.

Second, no quantitative method provides objective, automatic, and
ready-to-use outputs. Rather, the quantitative methods we use offer raw,
uninterpreted statistical results that systematically require
qualitative interpretation. For instance, in our analysis we use
bibliometric and textual techniques to group texts together. This is in
fact a classic strategy to reduce a large and complex set of texts to a
manageable number of simple categories. But these clusters are
constructed on the basis of statistical commonalities, whose actual
conceptual meaning can only be characterized through qualitative
assessment. More importantly, a good qualitative knowledge of the corpus
and of intellectual debates at stake are indispensable to make sense of
raw results. Thus, whether in the collection of data or their analysis,
quantitative methods require a constant back-and-forth with qualitative
reasoning.

This cross-referencing with previous readings, various indicators, and a
selective examination of relevant articles is all the more essential
given that the methods proposed here could be described as
“unsupervised.” In other words, there is no a priori supervision or
human labeling to guide the algorithmic classification; therefore, human
interpretation remains central to evaluating the validity and usefulness
of the output. Indeed, what is crucial in any application of
quantitative methods is the careful “validation” of the results, whether
through quantitative indicators or qualitative interpretation. In this
context, we need to assess whether the categories produced by our
methods—namely bibliometric intertemporal communities and meaning
clusters—constitute a relevant and helpful classification of our corpus.
A key issue here concerns the construction of indicators that help
analysts decide which documents should be read as a priority. Any
dashboard will depend on the corpus and the research context, but a
sound strategy is to rely on a combination of indicators rather than on
a single measure. It is also important to design indicators using
information available from the historical period under investigation in
order to avoid presentism. For instance, to understand a network
community from a past period, it is tempting to look first at the most
cited papers as a proxy for the community’s most important documents.
Yet this can be misleading, since total citation counts reflect current
popularity rather than what was influential at the time.

In the case of a large-scale study such as this one, most results are
not surprising—and there is nothing wrong with that. On the contrary,
given the large body of works that have contributed to the
historiography of rationality, one should expect our method to confirm
existing findings rather than to produce entirely new discoveries.
Precisely because much of what can be uncovered through quantitative
analysis has already, in some way, been identified by other means, these
methods can be trusted. This confirmation provides the basis for using
them to explore where the historiography is less developed. A couple of
patterns from our results can be highlighted as confirmations of
existing consensus in the historiography. The first example concerns the
story of how economics, through the development of rationality theory,
distanced itself from psychology (Giocoli 2003). By analyzing a selected
group of prominent economists from the first half of the twentieth
century—such as Vilfredo Pareto, Irving Fisher, Lionel Robbins, and Paul
Samuelson—Giocoli traces the long-standing debate on the relationship
between economics and psychology. This central debate on the role of
hedonism in explaining economic behavior is clearly reflected in Cluster
2 (Figure X, LLM alluvial), which extends from 1900 to the 1940s. The
cluster gathers discussions between proponents of hedonistic foundations
and their critics, such as institutionalists, who regarded this
psychological grounding as dubious. For instance, in this cluster, one
of the closest sentences to the representative vector of this is from
Wesley C. Mitchell, who argued that “to find the basis of economic
rationality in the development of a social institution directs our
attention away from that dark subjective realm, where so many economists
have groped, to an objective realm, where behavior can be studied in the
light of the common day” (Mitchell 1916, 160).

The 1940s and the 1950s also revealed the existence of two textual
clusters (which are relatively highly correlated together but not
sufficiently to be merged according to our threshold), which displayed
debates over economic freedom and free enterprise against economic
planning. Interestingly, we find in these clusters various roundtables
and special issues of essays discussing economic planning—see this
roundtable (Perroux…) on Lange’s (1949) “The Practice of Economic
Planning and The Optimum Allocation of Resources” (1949) involving
François Perroux, Jan Tinbergen, Evsey Domar or Michal Kalecki— or “the
proper spheres of individual freedom and collective control in the
‘good’ economy” (Taylor 1948)—in a collection of essays with among
others Henry Simons. In these two clusters, Frank Knight appears as the
most recurrent author.[^5] Somewhat linked to this is the textual
cluster 53, which from the 1950s on, discussed the issue of social
choices and welfare, with rationality being thought as a guide for
decision makers.[^6]

The postwar period also testified of intense debate about utility
theory, in textual cluster 31 for the 1940s, with notably Friedman and
Savage (1948), but above all after the 1950s with cluster 46. This
cluster discusses the demand theory and questioned in the first year the
use of cardinal utility and the possibility of intertemporal
comparisons. Chicago economics like Friedman and Savage (1952), Stigler
(1950) and, later on, Becker (1962) figure prominently in this group,
while Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen (1954) proposed a stark criticism of the
use of the concept of “utility” in economics, and the lack of a clear
definition of its measurability.

For the most “recent” period, a broad overview of our results makes two
very expected patterns. Whether in the bibliometric or textual analyses,
after the 1970s, rational expectations became a central concept that
occupies an important extent of discussion, represented by many textual
clusters or bibliometric communities (see below). Similarly, after the
1980s, the debate and undermining of the standard rationality approach
in economics, notably through the EUT, appeared recurrently in various
textual clusters (textual clusters 83 or 93) that persisted until the
end of our periods, while a clear behavioural economics cluster (106)
appears in the 2000s. In the XXIth century, these thematics have become
more prevalent than discussion on rational expectations. Something
similar is visible through bibliometric analysis where a first community
about “Behavioral Economics and Choice Theory” appeared in 1977-1984,
and many communities then popped up to form a complex network of
discussions around the modelling of rationality in economics after the
2000.[^7]

# **Discussion**

What can these complex quantitative methods and the resulting careful
interpretation bring about the history of rationality? How may it help
to enrich, complete and refine our understanding of the various and
evolving meanings of rationality in economics? As this paper aims mainly
at underlining concretely the interests, issues and uses of quantitative
methods in the history and philosophy of economics, our goal is not to
produce an alternative history of the concept of rationality, nor to
produce a comprehensive depiction of its evolution.

Rather, we would like to highlight what appears to us as interesting
pieces of results, confirming and strengthening some pieces of the
literature in the history of rationality, broadening this literature, as
well as, we hope, opening new paths and raising issues for further
research.

Mixing the various indicators with qualitative analysis (reading in
detail the different analyses produced from our methods and using the
literature).

Our goal is thus also to illustrate how we “navigate” our results, cross
different indicators, to produce interesting insights and narratives.

## The stabilisation of the concept of rationality

Before diving into the interpretation of the clusters, the structure of
the alluvial in Figure X (alluvial LLM) already reveals an important
insight. In the first half of the 20th century, many clusters appeared
and disappeared quickly, reflecting a certain instability. From the
second half of the century onward, however, clusters become more stable
and persist over time, indicating a clearer consolidation of meanings
and uses.

1)  A rational expectations revolution ?

One way to look at our results is to focus on one specific concept, more
accurately formalised and with less possible meanings than
“rationality”, i.e. “rational expectations”. The concept has an
interesting early history: developed by John Muth in 1960 to account for
price setting in agriculture, it gained popularity when being grasped by
Muth’s colleagues at Carnegie Tech, Robert Lucas, Edward Prescott and
Thomas Sargent, who applied it to macroeconomics, in a context far from
Muth’s original application. That’s only in the early 1970s that
rational expectations became an important concept in economics, soon
becoming quite controversial, notably because of its consequences when
applied to monetary or fiscal policies. At the end of the 1970s, the
concept was also circulating in policy circles and newspapers, the
latter claiming about an “Rational Expectations Revolution”.

What our methods may be helpful to is for understanding the quick
diffusion of the assumption in economics, beyond its controversial
popularity linked to the debates over macroeconomic policies in a
context of stagflation in the 1970s.

First, the results support, indirectly, that rational expectation gained
popularity only in the 1970s, when applied to macroeconomics. Indeed,
the concept of rational expectations is absent from the 1960s both in
the bibliometric and textual results. As early as the 1970s, it occupied
a central place in the literature dealing with rationality.[^8]

The controversial dimension of rational expectations is visible first
through text analysis. Two textual clusters about rational expectations
emerged in the 1970s decade (Textual clusters n° 67 and 72). The first
one is populated by articles discussing in-depth the rational
expectations hypothesis.[^9] In this perspective, many articles are
criticizing or questioning the theoretical or empirical relevance of
rational expectations in the 1970s and 1980s (e.g.,...). Others are
discussing the implication of the use of this hypothesis for various
domains (examples…). The second one rather deals with the models using
rational expectations, rather than the hypothesis in itself.[^10] Here
again, in the first decades, in parallel with the promotion of the
rational expectations model (Sargent is one of the major authors of the
cluster), we find several criticisms of these models, for their
incorporation of the hypothesis, but also for the other hypothesis used
in complement. The best example is perhaps Ray Fair’s (1978, 411)
criticism of “one class of macroeconomics models that have recently been
developed”, these models relying on “(1) the assumption that
expectations are rational, given the available information; (2) the
assumption that information is imperfect regarding the current state of
the economy; and (3) the postulation of an aggregate supply equation in
which aggregate supply is a function of exogenous terms plus the
diSerence between the actual and expected price level.”[^11] The large
diffusion of is also visible through clusters that exist before rational
expectations is used, but which then incorporate them, especially in the
1980s (ie the textual cluster 76 on monetary economics issues and the
cluster 28, a cluster dating back from the 1940s, focusing on the theory
of prices).[^12]

Our bibliometric analysis offers a fine-grained approach to complement
text analysis and to reveal some similar patterns but by other means: by
focusing on referencing rather than textual use, and by relying on
overlapping windows, it allows to observe with accuracy the emergence of
new communities or the split of others. The main bibliometric community
on rational expectations, which appears for the first time in 1966-1973,
does not deal primarily with the treatment of the hypothesis in itself,
but its implications for macroeconomic policy. Here, the controversy is
not so much about the relevance of the hypothesis, but about its use in
the modelling of the inflation-unemployment trade-off, and its
consequences in terms of (in-)efficiency of monetary policy. Here, we
retrieve the early opposition between the “old” and (future) “new”
Keynesians (Goutsmedt et al., 2019).

The controversial aspect of rational expectations in the 1970s and 1980s
likely helps to explain its “prevalence” of this community in our
results. These controversies have been well covered by the literature on
the subject (Ref). But, relying on our results, we can also argue that
rational expectations have spread in economics through a process of
diffusion by being applied to various economic problems. Relying on
bibliometric analysis, this could be seen through two schematic types of
diffusion. First, communities that were independent from the main
rational expectations community (“Rational Expectations and Business
Cycles”) started to use rational expectations. Let’s delve into the some
communities that may represent these two types of diffusion process.
Second, the appearance of new communities, which are outgrowing the main
rational expectations community appearing in the 1970s. Here, the papers
in these new communities are initially in the rational expectations
community, and progressively autonomize, with new communities appearing,
becoming autonomous from the initial one.

Regarding the first category, it’s interesting to see that actually, one
community invested the issue of rational expectations well before the
“Rational Expectations and Business Cycle” community. This community
dealt with various subjects related to trade, demand or investment, but
with a general equilibrium theory framework. Muth (1961)’s was part of
this community. Later on it remains one of the important references of
the community, even if rational expectations hypothesis was not totally
central to it. In 1971-1978, this community becomes “Investment and
Economic Growth”. In this community, Lucas' first papers on investment
played an important role (but these papers did not use rational
expectations). Again, if rational expectations was not totally central
to the community which mainly dealt with firms’ investment and
adjustment costs, many significant references used rational
expectations, like Cyert and DeGroot’s “Rational Expectations and
Bayesian Analysis” (Ref) or Townsend’s (1978). In 1975-1982, it became
“Investment and Uncertainty”. Even if they were not “central nodes” to
the community, this community welcomed Kydland and Prescott (1977, 1982)
and Lucas (1978).[^13]

Beyond this parallel path of rational expectations in addition to the
well-known debates on business cycles and inflation, we find after the
1970s several trajectories of independent communities that start to

  rational expectations, notably citing the works of K&P 77 and Barro &
  Gordon

Outside of the investment community that was here from the beginning,
other breaks in the network analysis:

- exchange rate and monetary policy

- inflation and interest rates expectations - typical literature on the
  use of RE to predict inflation

- Emergence of the implicit contracts and wages rigidity in 1977-1986.
  More known, as it would formed partly the basis for “New Keynesian
  economics” (comes mainly from disequilibrium).

This issue of rational expectations diffusion would deserve a whole
paper. The goal here was uniquely to show the diversity of trajectories
and the fine-grained mapping that our analyses produce, opening
possibilities of rich interaction between quantitative data, selective
text reading and qualitative approaches.

2)  … from bounded rationality to Behavioral econ? Challenging standard
    rationality and expected utility

It is well known that if Simon’s “bounded rationality” constitutes one
of the most famous concepts related to rationality, and supported a
significant criticism of the standard treatment of rationality in
economics, its success was delayed in time, well after Simon’s (1955,
1959) article. However, our bibliometric and textual analyses allow us
to explore in detail the trajectory of Simon’s concept.

For sure, Simon was an important character of the debates about
rationality in the 1950s, and we can find his two seminal articles and
his Nobel lecture (Simon, 1979) featured in good places in almost a
dozen of textual clusters (on social choice, firm behavior, price
setting, etc…), testifying of how its discussion of economic rationality
echoed a large specter of debates on this issue. However, if its
contribution had already got the highest graal in economics in the late
1970s, his concepts of “bounded rationality”, “procedural rationality”,
and “satisficing” remained marginal at this time. The Figure X above on
Simon (1955) citations in economics testifies of its late reckoning, the
article being increasingly cited after the 1970s, but only to grasp a
significant share of citations after the 1980s.

The textual analysis offers perhaps an even more striking proof. Textual
cluster 40, one of the biggest clusters of our textual analysis,
aggregated over 70 years, from 1950 on, general discussion on
rationality in economics. In the 1950s, if we find Simon (1955) as a
recurrent article in this cluster, the discussion mainly turned around
rationality in game theory—with contributions, for instance, by Thomas
Schelling (1959) or Daniel Ellsberg (1956)—and expected utility
theory—with contributions by Jacob Marschak (1950) and Herman Chernoff
(1954). What happens next…

The bibliometric approach, with successive time windows, allows to
follow closely even the smallest communities. And that’s what allows us
to follow the influence of Simon’s 1950s contributions, which appear
quite reduced at first. In the first window (1960-1967), Simon (1959) is
cited in a community with operational research at its heart (cl_5). In
parallel to operational research, this community which persisted—but
reduced in size—until 1969-1976, was progressively populated by
organizational theory articles criticizing the hypothesis of firm’s
profit-maximization in neoclassical models.. Two main examples here are
Sydney Winter (1971), applying Simon’s satisficing principle to study
firm’s behavior, or Richard Cyert (Simon’s colleague at Carnegie) and
Kenneth George (1969). Another important actor of this literature was
Harvey Leibenstein who proposed the concept of “X-efficiency”,
criticizing neoclassical economics's focus on allocative efficiency.
Simon, Winter, Cyert, and Leibenstein constituted a relatively
heterogenous group of organizational theorists critique of the use of
the rationality concept, notably through profit-maximization in
economics.

After 1969-1976, this group will land in a smaller community (cl_175)
which will be short-lived. References to Simon and this kind of
criticisms of profit-maximization will remain coerced but will navigate
through various small communities (cl_182, cl_251, cl_300 and cl_328).
This instability underlined the marginal nature of this literature,
often associated shortly with other types of contributions.

Eventually merged with other criticism of firms. But also ending with
the new behavioural economics cluster, before becoming truly what will
be known as behavioural economics. Then, no clusters display significant
citations to Simon’s contributions, even if the concept of bounded
rationality will pop-up in various communities, the best example in the
1990s being Selten (1990) in the “Behavioral Theory” cluster.

[^1]: One of the main challenges for a quantitative history of economics
    is to move beyond reliance on proprietary digital libraries and to
    actively develop open, historically inclusive corpora. This includes
    incorporating materials produced in non-Anglophone countries and
    expanding the range of textual formats considered—such as books,
    book reviews, working papers, and conference proceedings.

[^2]: The intuition behind word embedding is the distributional
    hypothesis, famously stated by the linguist John R. Firth (1957):
    “you shall know a word by the company it keeps”.

[^3]: One issue with using LLMs is that they are pre-trained on recent
    data, which raises the methodological problem of *presentism*.
    Contextualized embeddings partially mitigate this issue, as the
    vectorization of texts depends on the immediate linguistic context.
    As illustrated in Table 1, each historical period is associated with
    its own specific set of questions and, therefore, with particular
    contextual usages of the term *rationality*. However, the way these
    surrounding words influence the vector representation of
    *rationality* remains shaped by a bias toward present-day language
    and meanings. This limitation is discussed further in the
    conclusion.¹

[^4]: Sophisticated techniques used in the history of economics—whether
    topic modeling, network analysis, or contextual embeddings—often
    depend on modeling choices (for example, the number of topics in a
    topic model) that can substantially affect the output. Since these
    outputs are never self-interpreting and always require human
    qualitative assessment, it is always very costly to conduct
    robustness checks.

[^5]: See also textual cluster 31 on planning issues,

[^6]: Kenneth Arrow, Herbert Simon or James Buchanan are central in
    these debates.

[^7]: See for instance the communities “Behavioral Economics and
    Experiments”, “Ambiguity and Uncertainty”, “Intertemporal Choice and

[^8]: This reveals one important possible caveat of such methods: as
    they tend to display “significant” patterns, it does not work well
    for tracing and understanding carefully the origins of some concept
    or theory, as historical studies and archives can do.

[^9]: That’s one of the strengths of our textual method: it does not
    simply identify sentences that mention the topic which is of
    interest to us (rationality, and more specifically, here, rational
    expectations); but it rather finds sentences which significantly
    *engage* the topic.

[^12]: Other textual clusters linked to rational expectations are
